parts.context: Two volunteers who organize a youth soccer tournament are dealing with a problem.

lines: Shauna, I just drove past Centennial Park. Fields three and four are under water. The storm last night must have flooded the whole lower section.
You’re joking. The tournament starts at nine tomorrow morning. We’ve got sixteen teams coming, some from two hours away.

I know. I called the parks department, and they said even if it stops raining, those fields won’t be playable for at least three days. Playing on them wet would tear up the grass, and the city would charge us for the damage.
What about fields one and two? They’re on higher ground.
They’re fine. But two fields isn’t enough for sixteen teams. We planned twenty-four games on four fields.
So we’d have half the space. Could we just make the games shorter?
I thought about that. If we cut each game from fifty minutes to thirty, we could fit more in, but the parents have paid ninety dollars per team. They won’t be happy if their kids barely play.
True. And the younger kids need breaks anyway. Okay, let’s think about other places.
There’s the community centre gym, but it’s indoors and only big enough for one small-sided game at a time. And they want three hundred dollars for the day.
No, that won’t help much. We’d be paying a lot for one tiny space. I’d rather spend that money on a proper field.

qs.q: Why can’t fields three and four be used?
o: They are being repaired by the city.
They were booked by another league.
They were flooded by heavy rain.
They are too far from the parking lot.
qs.ev: Fields three and four are under water
qs.x: Bruno says fields three and four are under water after last night’s storm. The city is involved only because it would charge for damage, not because it is repairing the fields.

qs.q: What would happen if they played on the wet fields?
o: The players might get sick.
The games would be cancelled.
Referees would refuse to work.
They could be charged for damage.
qs.ev: the city would charge us for the damage
qs.x: The parks department warned that playing on wet fields would tear up the grass and the city would charge them for the damage. Nobody mentions players getting sick or referees refusing.

qs.q: Why does Bruno reject shortening the games?
o: Families who paid would feel their kids played too little.
The referees would not accept thirty-minute games.
The tournament rules set games at fifty minutes.
It would still not fit twenty-four games in.
qs.ev: They won’t be happy if their kids barely play
qs.x: Bruno says each team paid ninety dollars and parents won’t be happy if their kids barely play. He admits shorter games would let them fit more in, so a lack of time saved is wrong.

lines: What about the high school? They have an artificial turf field.
Good idea, turf drains fast. But it’s a weekend. Would anyone even answer?
The athletic director, Mr. Haddad, coaches my son’s basketball team. I have his cell number. Let me call him now.
While you do that, I’ll check the Catholic school on Pine. They have two grass fields, but they’re smaller, more like under-ten size.
That might actually work for the youngest division. Okay, calling Haddad. … Hi, Mr. Haddad, it’s Shauna Kelly… Yes… I’m sorry to bother you on a Friday night…
Good news. He says the turf field is free tomorrow, but the school board requires proof of insurance and a custodian on site, which costs forty-five dollars an hour. He can email the form tonight.
The league insurance covers any venue, so that’s easy. A custodian for eight hours is three hundred and sixty dollars, though.
We have about five hundred left in the budget after the trophies. It’s tight, but it’s doable.
Doable, but it means no pizza for the volunteers on Sunday.
They’ll survive. I’ll bring muffins. Can you call the referees, too? They need to know about the new venue so they can plan their drives.
I’ll text the head referee. She assigns everyone, so she can pass it on.

qs.q: Why is the high school field a good option?
o: It is the closest to Centennial Park.
Its artificial surface dries quickly.
It is free on weekends.
It has lights for evening games.
qs.ev: turf drains fast
qs.x: Bruno says turf drains fast, so the field will be usable after the storm. It is “free” tomorrow only in the sense of available; using it still costs money for a custodian.

qs.q: How might the Catholic school fields be used?
o: For the older divisions’ games
For extra parking on Saturday
For the youngest players’ games
For the awards and trophies
qs.ev: That might actually work for the youngest division
qs.x: The Catholic school fields are smaller, under-ten size, so Shauna says they might work for the youngest division. The older divisions will play at Centennial and on the high school turf.

qs.q: What is required to use the high school field?
o: Insurance documents and a paid custodian
A rental fee per team
Permission from the city
A signed contract with the parks department
qs.ev: the school board requires proof of insurance and a custodian on site
qs.x: Mr. Haddad says the school board requires proof of insurance and a custodian on site at forty-five dollars an hour. No per-team fee or parks department contract is mentioned.

lines: Okay, so the plan: the older divisions play on fields one and two at Centennial and on the high school turf. If the Catholic school agrees, the under-tens go there.
But now teams are spread over three locations. Parents will get confused.
Right. We need to send a new schedule tonight with a map, and put signs at Centennial in case people show up there anyway.
I’ll do the schedule. And I’ll ask two volunteers to stand in the Centennial parking lot in the morning to redirect people.
Perfect. I’ll call the Catholic school first thing, at seven. If they say no, the under-tens will just play shorter games on Centennial field two.
That works. And what about the teams coming from two hours away? Some of them might have left by the time they read the email.
Good point. I’ll phone those four coaches directly tonight. It’s only four calls.
And let’s keep the start time at nine everywhere. If we change locations and times, nobody will get it right.
Agreed. Nine o’clock at all three sites. I’ll also ask Mr. Haddad if teams can use the school washrooms. Otherwise we’ll need portable toilets, and those take a day’s notice.

qs.q: What is Shauna worried about?
o: The cost of a custodian for eight hours
Rain flooding the high school field too
Running out of money after buying trophies
Parents getting mixed up about where to go
qs.ev: Parents will get confused
qs.x: Shauna points out that teams are now spread over three locations and parents will get confused. The custodian cost was discussed earlier, and she said the budget was tight but doable.

qs.q: What will happen if the Catholic school says no?
o: The tournament will be postponed until the fields dry.
The youngest teams will play shorter games at Centennial.
All the teams will move to the high school turf field.
The under-tens will play full games at the high school.
qs.ev: the under-tens will just play shorter games on Centennial field two
qs.x: Bruno says that if the Catholic school refuses, the under-tens will play shorter games on Centennial field two. Shorter games were rejected for everyone but are accepted as a backup for the youngest.

parts.context: A customer is speaking with an agent at a car rental counter.

lines: Hi there, do you have a reservation?
Yes, under Mehta. A compact car for four days.
Let me see. Yes, Mr. Mehta. I should let you know that we’re out of compact cars this morning, so we’ll be upgrading you to a mid-size sedan at no extra cost.
Oh, that’s nice. Will it use more gas?
A little, but not much. It’s a hybrid, so it might actually use less. Now, would you like to add our collision coverage? It’s twenty-nine dollars a day.
I think my credit card covers rental cars. Is that enough?

Many cards do include it, but some exclude certain vehicles or rentals longer than a set number of days. I’d recommend checking with your card company. If you decline our coverage and your card doesn’t cover it, you’d be responsible for the full cost of any damage.
I checked before I came. My card covers rentals up to thirty-one days for standard cars, and it says a mid-size sedan is fine.
Great, then you can decline. I’ll just need you to initial here. Will anyone else be driving?

Additional drivers are twelve dollars a day, but spouses are free in this province. She’ll need to show her licence when she picks up the keys or before she drives, though. You can bring her by any of our locations.
It comes with a full tank. Bring it back full, or we charge two dollars and ten cents per litre, which is quite a bit more than the gas station across the street.
I’ll fill it up, then. One last question: if my flight home is delayed, can I return the car a few hours late?
There’s a thirty-minute grace period. After that, we charge for an extra day. If you call us before your return time, though, we can usually extend it at the hourly rate instead.

qs.q: Why is Mr. Mehta getting a different car?
o: He asked for a larger car when booking.
He wanted a car that uses less gas.
There are no compact cars available.
His reservation was for a mid-size car.
qs.ev: we’re out of compact cars this morning
qs.x: The agent says they are out of compact cars this morning, so he is upgraded for free. He asks about gas only after hearing about the upgrade, so he did not request a hybrid.

qs.q: Why does the agent suggest contacting the credit card company?
o: Card coverage may have exceptions.
The card will be charged extra.
The card has expired.
The company offers a discount.
qs.ev: some exclude certain vehicles or rentals longer than a set number of days
qs.x: The agent says some cards exclude certain vehicles or longer rentals, so the coverage may not apply. A deposit or a discount from the card company is never mentioned.

qs.q: Why does Mr. Mehta decline the collision coverage?
o: Twenty-nine dollars a day is too expensive.
He has already checked that his card covers it.
He only plans to drive short distances.
The agent tells him that it is not needed for sedans.
qs.ev: it says a mid-size sedan is fine
qs.x: Mr. Mehta says he checked before coming and his card covers mid-size sedans for up to thirty-one days. The agent actually recommends checking with the card company, not declining the coverage.

qs.q: What must Mr. Mehta’s wife do before driving?
o: Pay twelve dollars a day
Sign a separate contract
Buy collision coverage
Show her driver’s licence
qs.ev: She’ll need to show her licence
qs.x: The agent says his wife must show her licence before driving. The twelve-dollar daily fee applies to other additional drivers, but spouses are free in this province.

qs.q: What does the agent imply about refuelling?
o: The car should be brought back with an empty tank.
Fuel for the four days is included in the price.
Filling up yourself before returning costs less.
The gas station across the street charges more.
qs.ev: which is quite a bit more than the gas station across the street
qs.x: The agent says the rental charge of $2.10 per litre is quite a bit more than the gas station across the street, implying refuelling there is cheaper. The station is not the expensive option.

parts.context: A newcomer is meeting with an employment counsellor at a settlement agency.

lines: So, Tariq, you were an electrical engineer in your home country for eleven years. That’s great experience. Let’s talk about how to get it recognized here.
Yes. I’ve applied for many engineering jobs, but nobody calls me back.

That’s very common, unfortunately. In Canada, engineering is a regulated profession. You can’t call yourself a professional engineer without a licence from the provincial engineering association. Employers often filter out applications from people who aren’t licensed, or at least on the way.
How long does a licence take?

It varies, but often one to two years. First, the association assesses your degree. If it’s from a recognized program, you might not need to write extra exams. You also need to pass an exam on professional practice and law, and show twelve months of Canadian engineering experience, under the supervision of a licensed engineer.
But how can I get Canadian experience if no one hires me without a licence?

That’s the classic problem. There are a few routes. Many people start in related roles, like engineering technologist or project coordinator, which don’t require a licence. Those jobs often count towards the experience requirement if a licensed engineer supervises your work.
That makes sense. Is there any help with the cost? The fees are quite high.

There is a provincial bridging program for internationally trained engineers. It’s free for eligible newcomers, it includes a paid four-month work placement, and it covers the exam fees. The next intake is in September, and applications close at the end of June.
That sounds perfect. What do I need to apply?

Your degree transcripts, which must be sent directly from your university, and proof of English at a certain level. Since you’ve just done a language test, you may already have that. Let’s also update your résumé to the Canadian format. Yours is five pages; we’ll aim for two.
Two pages? I’ll have to leave out a lot of projects.

Employers here often spend less than a minute on a first read, so we’ll keep the most relevant projects and put the rest on your professional networking profile. Also, take off your photo and date of birth. That’s standard practice in many countries, but here it isn’t expected.
I didn’t know that. Should I mention the licence process on the résumé?
Yes. Once you’ve applied, add a line saying you’re in the process of licensing with the provincial association. It shows employers you’re on the way.

qs.q: Why might Tariq not be getting calls from employers?
o: He does not yet have a professional licence.
His eleven years abroad are not enough experience.
His English test results are not high enough.
He is applying for the wrong positions.
qs.ev: Employers often filter out applications from people who aren’t licensed
qs.x: The counsellor explains that employers often filter out applicants who are not licensed or on the way to a licence. His eleven years of experience is described as great, not limited.

qs.q: What is required to become licensed?
o: A degree from a Canadian engineering school
Five years of experience under a licensed engineer
Twelve months of supervised Canadian experience
A permanent job offer from a Canadian employer
qs.ev: show twelve months of Canadian engineering experience, under the supervision of a licensed engineer
qs.x: Licensing requires twelve months of Canadian experience supervised by a licensed engineer, plus a practice exam. A degree from a recognized program abroad can be accepted, so a Canadian degree is not required.

qs.q: How does the counsellor suggest Tariq gain Canadian experience?
o: By volunteering at an engineering firm overseas
By returning to university for a Canadian degree
By starting his own consulting business here
By taking related jobs that don’t need a licence
qs.ev: Many people start in related roles, like engineering technologist or project coordinator
qs.x: She suggests starting in related roles such as technologist or project coordinator, which need no licence and can count as experience if supervised. Returning to university is never suggested.

qs.q: What does the bridging program offer?
o: A low-interest loan for tuition
Free training with a paid work placement
A guaranteed job after four months
A faster route to a full licence
qs.ev: it includes a paid four-month work placement, and it covers the exam fees
qs.x: The bridging program is free for eligible newcomers, includes a paid four-month work placement and covers exam fees. The four months refer to the placement, not a guaranteed job afterwards.

qs.q: When must Tariq apply for the bridging program?
o: In September
Within twelve months
By the end of June
After he receives his licence
qs.ev: applications close at the end of June
qs.x: Applications close at the end of June for the September intake. September is when the program starts, so applying then would be too late.

qs.q: What does the counsellor say about Tariq’s résumé?
o: It is too short for an engineer with his experience.
It is too long for what employers here expect.
It should be sent directly from his university.
It should include his photo and date of birth.
qs.ev: Yours is five pages; we’ll aim for two
qs.x: His résumé is five pages and the counsellor wants two, the Canadian format. Transcripts, not the résumé, must come directly from the university, and the photo and birth date should be removed.

parts.context: You will hear a news report.

lines: Residents who buy an electric bicycle will soon be eligible for a rebate of up to six hundred dollars, under a new program announced by the city today.

The rebate covers twenty-five percent of the purchase price, up to the six-hundred-dollar limit, and applies only to bikes bought from local retailers. Residents with a household income under fifty thousand dollars can receive up to twelve hundred. The city says it has set aside enough money for about two thousand rebates in the first year, on a first-come, first-served basis.

The goal is to reduce short car trips. According to city data, almost half of all car trips in the city are under five kilometres, a distance that most people can easily cover on an e-bike, even in hilly areas.
Local bike shops say interest is already high. Gina Russo, who owns a shop on Queen Street, expects demand to jump.

We’re already getting calls. My only concern is supply. If two thousand people come in during the first month, we simply won’t have enough bikes in stock. I’d tell people not to panic-buy. The money isn’t going to vanish overnight.
And people should remember that the rebate only works at local shops. If they order online from another province, they won’t get a cent back.

Some critics argue that the rebate mainly benefits people who could already afford an e-bike, and that the money would be better spent on protected bike lanes. City officials respond that the program includes funding for one hundred new secure bike parking spaces at transit stations, and that both bikes and infrastructure are needed.
Applications open on the first of next month. Residents will need to submit a receipt and proof of address within sixty days of their purchase.

qs.q: How much can most residents receive?
o: Half of the price, up to $1,200 in total
A fixed $600 for any bike bought locally
A quarter of the price, up to $600
Up to $1,200 for any resident who applies
qs.ev: The rebate covers twenty-five percent of the purchase price, up to the six-hundred-dollar limit
qs.x: Most residents get twenty-five percent of the price, up to six hundred dollars. The $1,200 limit applies only to households with incomes under fifty thousand dollars, not to every resident.

qs.q: Why does the city want to encourage e-bikes?
o: To support the tourism industry
To replace short car trips
To reduce noise downtown
To help local bike shops
qs.ev: The goal is to reduce short car trips
qs.x: The goal is to reduce short car trips, since almost half of car trips are under five kilometres. Local shops benefit from sales, but helping them is not the stated goal.

qs.q: What is Gina Russo’s main concern?
o: Many customers will not qualify for it.
The rebate is too small to matter.
People will buy their bikes online instead.
Shops may run short of bikes to sell.
qs.ev: we simply won’t have enough bikes in stock
qs.x: Gina says that if two thousand people come in during the first month, shops won’t have enough bikes in stock. She mentions online orders only to remind people they would not qualify.

qs.q: What does Gina Russo advise residents?
o: Not to rush their purchase
To buy quickly before the money runs out
To wait for next year’s program
To order from large online stores
qs.ev: I’d tell people not to panic-buy
qs.x: Gina tells people not to panic-buy because the money is not going to vanish overnight. Buying quickly before funds run out is exactly the panic-buying she warns against.

qs.q: How do city officials respond to critics?
o: They plan to replace the rebate with bike lanes.
They say protected bike lanes are too expensive.
They admit the program mainly helps the rich.
They point to investment in bike parking as well.
qs.ev: the program includes funding for one hundred new secure bike parking spaces at transit stations
qs.x: Officials answer that the program also funds one hundred secure bike parking spaces at transit stations and that bikes and infrastructure are both needed. They do not concede that it favours the wealthy.

parts.context: Three siblings are discussing the family cottage.

lines: Okay, we need to talk about the cottage. Since Dad passed, it’s been sitting empty most of the year, and the property taxes and insurance alone are almost nine thousand dollars a year. Plus the roof needs replacing.
I think we should sell it. I live in Calgary, so I get there maybe one week a year. It doesn’t make sense for me to pay a third of the costs for one week.
I understand that, Mark. But that cottage is where we spent every summer growing up. My kids learned to swim in that lake. Selling it would feel like losing Dad all over again.
I’m not saying it’s easy. I’m saying it’s expensive, and the roof alone is going to be fifteen thousand.
Could we do the roof in stages? The contractor said the back section is the worst.
He also said doing it in stages would cost about twenty percent more overall. I asked.
What if we rented it out? Cottages on that lake rent for about two thousand a week in summer. Even ten weeks would cover the taxes, insurance and part of the roof.
Strangers in Dad’s cottage? I don’t love that idea.
I don’t love it either. But it might be the difference between keeping it and losing it.
Renting also means someone has to manage it. Cleaning, keys, repairs. That’s not something I can do from Calgary.
I live forty minutes away. I could manage it, at least for the first summer. If it’s too much, we could hire a property manager. They take about twenty percent.
Twenty percent of twenty thousand is four thousand. That’s a big bite.
It is, but we’d still come out ahead, as long as we actually rent most of those ten weeks. The first summer, nobody knows the place.
Then we price it a little lower to start and ask the first renters for reviews. That’s how my neighbour did it.
Okay. If Elise is willing to manage it, I’m open to trying it for one season. But I want to set a clear review point. If after one summer we’re still losing money, we sell.
That seems fair. And what about the time we use it ourselves?
We keep two weeks in July for the family, like always. That’s non-negotiable for me.
Of course. Dad would have wanted that.
Fine. And one more thing: if one of us wants to buy the others out at some point, we should get it appraised so it’s fair.
Agreed. So: rent it out for the rest of the summer, Elise manages it, we keep two weeks in July, and we review in October.
And I’ll take photos this weekend, before the leaves start falling. Good pictures make a huge difference, and I’ll write a short guide to the lake for guests.
Just don’t promise anyone the dock. It needs a few new boards before anyone walks on it.

qs.q: Why does Mark want to sell the cottage?
o: He needs his share of the money right away.
He no longer enjoys spending time at the lake.
He pays a full share but barely uses it.
The roof is too damaged to be worth repairing.
qs.ev: It doesn’t make sense for me to pay a third of the costs for one week
qs.x: Mark lives in Calgary, visits about one week a year, and says paying a third of the costs makes no sense. He complains the roof is expensive, not that it cannot be repaired.

qs.q: Why is Elise against selling?
o: She hopes to retire there one day.
It has strong emotional value for her.
She expects its value to keep rising.
Her children want to learn to swim there.
qs.ev: Selling it would feel like losing Dad all over again
qs.x: Elise says selling would feel like losing Dad all over again, showing emotional attachment. Her kids already learned to swim in the lake; that is a memory, not a future plan.

qs.q: Why does Hannah suggest renting it out?
o: To find a buyer among the renters
To raise its value before a sale
To give Elise a summer job
To cover the costs and help keep it
qs.ev: it might be the difference between keeping it and losing it
qs.x: Hannah says ten weeks of rent would cover taxes, insurance and part of the roof, which might be the difference between keeping and losing it. She does not suggest renting as preparation for a sale.

qs.q: What is Mark’s concern about renting?
o: Someone nearby would need to run it day to day.
Renters might damage Dad’s old furniture.
Renting is not allowed by the lake association.
It would not earn enough to cover the roof.
qs.ev: Renting also means someone has to manage it
qs.x: Mark says renting means someone has to manage cleaning, keys and repairs, which he cannot do from Calgary. It is Elise, not Mark, who dislikes strangers in the cottage, and furniture is never mentioned.

qs.q: What does Elise offer to do?
o: Buy the cottage from her siblings
Pay for the new roof herself
Manage the rental herself at first
Hire a property manager now
qs.ev: I could manage it, at least for the first summer
qs.x: Elise lives forty minutes away and offers to manage it, at least for the first summer. A property manager is only a fallback if managing it becomes too much.

qs.q: What condition does Mark set?
o: They sell if renting still loses money after one season.
The cottage must be sold within a year regardless of profit.
He must get the cottage for two weeks every August.
Elise must pay for any repairs out of her own share.
qs.ev: If after one summer we’re still losing money, we sell
qs.x: Mark agrees to try renting for one season but insists they sell if they are still losing money after one summer. He sets no automatic one-year sale and makes no request for August.

qs.q: What is Elise unwilling to give up?
o: Managing the cottage for the first summer
Two weeks of family time in July
Her father’s old furniture
Keeping strangers out of the cottage
qs.ev: We keep two weeks in July for the family, like always. That’s non-negotiable for me.
qs.x: Elise says keeping two family weeks in July is non-negotiable. She dislikes having strangers there but accepts renting, and she offers to manage it rather than insisting on it.

qs.q: Why does Mark want an appraisal if one sibling buys out the others?
o: To increase the rent
To satisfy the bank
To lower the property taxes
To ensure a fair price
qs.ev: we should get it appraised so it’s fair
qs.x: Mark says that if one sibling buys out the others, they should get an appraisal so the price is fair. Taxes and rent are discussed, but not as reasons for an appraisal.

parts.context: You will hear a radio report about daylight saving time.

lines: Twice a year, most Canadians change their clocks, and twice a year, the same debate returns: should we stop? Several provinces have passed laws to adopt permanent daylight saving time, but most have made the change conditional on neighbouring provinces and U.S. states doing the same, so for now, the clocks keep changing.

Nearly everyone agrees that switching back and forth is a problem. Studies have found small increases in car accidents and heart attacks in the days after the spring change, when people lose an hour of sleep. The real disagreement is about which time to keep.
Some insurance companies also report a rise in claims during the same week, although the effect fades quickly.

Many politicians and business groups favour permanent daylight time, meaning brighter evenings all year. They argue that people would shop, exercise and socialize more after work, and that evening traffic would be safer. But many sleep scientists strongly prefer the opposite: permanent standard time.

Our bodies set their internal clocks mainly from morning light. With permanent daylight time, in parts of Canada the sun wouldn’t rise until after nine thirty in December. Children would be going to school in the dark for months. Over time, that mismatch is linked to poorer sleep, lower mood and worse concentration.
And it isn’t only children. Shift workers and people in the western part of each time zone would be hit hardest, because their sunrise is already later.
She adds that most medical associations that have taken a position have backed permanent standard time.

Supporters of daylight time say those dark mornings would affect only a few months of the year, and that people adapt. Some point out that when the United States tried year-round daylight time in the nineteen seventies, it was popular at first but was abandoned within a year, largely because of complaints about dark winter mornings.
Business groups also note that retailers and restaurants report higher sales on bright evenings, and that outdoor sports leagues could schedule more games after work.
For now, any change seems unlikely without coordination across North America. In the meantime, sleep experts recommend going to bed fifteen minutes earlier for a few nights before the spring change.
Some provinces have also discussed simply staying on standard time all year, which would not require any neighbour’s approval, but so far none has moved ahead with that option.
Polls suggest most Canadians want to stop changing the clocks for good, but they are almost evenly split on which time to keep.

qs.q: Why have most provinces not yet stopped changing clocks?
o: Voters rejected the laws in provincial referendums.
Business groups lobbied against permanent daylight time.
Their laws only take effect if neighbours also change.
Sleep scientists asked them to wait for more studies.
qs.ev: most have made the change conditional on neighbouring provinces and U.S. states doing the same
qs.x: Most provinces made the change conditional on neighbouring provinces and U.S. states doing the same, so clocks still change. Business groups actually favour permanent daylight time rather than opposing it.

qs.q: What do most people agree on?
o: Daylight time should be made permanent everywhere.
Standard time is healthier for most children.
The spring change causes no real health effects.
Moving the clocks back and forth is harmful.
qs.ev: Nearly everyone agrees that switching back and forth is a problem
qs.x: The reporter says nearly everyone agrees switching back and forth is a problem; the disagreement is about which time to keep. So permanent daylight time is disputed, not agreed on.

qs.q: Why do business groups prefer permanent daylight time?
o: It would cut energy costs for stores and offices.
People would be more active in the evenings.
Mornings would be brighter for commuters.
It would match the time used in U.S. states.
qs.ev: people would shop, exercise and socialize more after work
qs.x: Supporters say brighter evenings would lead people to shop, exercise and socialize more after work. Brighter mornings are what permanent standard time offers, the option sleep scientists prefer.

qs.q: What is the sleep researcher’s main concern about permanent daylight time?
o: Late winter sunrises would hurt sleep, mood and focus.
Bright evenings would keep people awake too late at night.
Schools would have to start much later in the winter.
It would increase car accidents during dark evening drives.
qs.ev: With permanent daylight time, in parts of Canada the sun wouldn’t rise until after nine thirty in December
qs.x: The researcher says the body sets its clock from morning light, and December sunrises after nine-thirty would harm sleep, mood and concentration. She never complains about bright evenings.

qs.q: Why does the reporter mention the United States in the 1970s?
o: To prove that permanent daylight time stays popular over time
To explain how daylight time first started in North America
To show a past trial of the idea that was soon dropped
To compare American and Canadian attitudes toward the clocks
qs.ev: it was popular at first but was abandoned within a year
qs.x: The U.S. tried year-round daylight time in the 1970s; it was popular at first but abandoned within a year because of dark winter mornings. So it does not prove the idea stays popular.

qs.q: What do sleep experts recommend?
o: Avoiding driving for a few days after the change
Shifting bedtime earlier for a few nights in advance
Sleeping an extra hour on the night of the fall change
Using bright lights in the evenings before the change
qs.ev: going to bed fifteen minutes earlier for a few nights before the spring change

p1.text:
Dear Mr. Osei,

Thank you for taking the time to meet with our team last week. I am delighted to offer you the position of Warehouse Supervisor at our Mississauga distribution centre, reporting to me.

The position is full-time and permanent, with an annual salary of $68,500. You will be eligible for our group health and dental benefits after three months of employment, and you will receive three weeks of paid vacation in your first year. As discussed, the role involves supervising a team of fourteen on the evening shift, from 3:00 p.m. to 11:30 p.m., Monday to Friday. For working evenings, you will receive an additional shift premium of $1.50 per hour. Your team includes two lead hands who have been with us for several years and will be a great support as you settle in.

During your interview, you asked about the possibility of moving to the day shift. While I cannot promise a specific date, we expect a day supervisor position to open within the next year as part of our expansion, and internal candidates are always considered first.

We would like you to start on Monday, March 3. Your first week will be spent on the day shift, shadowing our current day supervisor, so that you can learn our systems and meet the management team. You will also need to complete forklift safety certification, which we provide on site at no cost during your first month. Staff parking is free, and the centre is a ten-minute walk from the Northgate bus terminal.

This offer is conditional on a satisfactory background check and verification of your references. Please sign and return the attached contract by February 14. If you have any questions about the terms, do not hesitate to contact me directly.

We are very pleased to welcome you to the Northwind team.

Sincerely,
Deborah Kwan

p3.title: The End of the Drive-Through?
paras: For decades, the drive-through has been a symbol of North American convenience. Customers can order coffee, burgers or even prescriptions without leaving their cars. During the pandemic, drive-throughs became more popular than ever, and many restaurants added second lanes to handle the demand. Chains redesigned their buildings around them, and some new locations opened with no indoor seating at all. Banks, pharmacies and even some dry cleaners have offered drive-through service too. For many commuters, picking up breakfast without leaving the car became part of the daily routine.

Yet a growing number of municipalities are now restricting new drive-throughs. Some have banned them in downtown areas or near schools, while others require a special permit and a traffic study before one can be built. Supporters of the restrictions point to idling cars, which produce emissions while waiting, and to long lines that spill onto streets and block sidewalks and bike lanes. In one Ontario city, police were called repeatedly to a coffee shop whose drive-through queue regularly backed up onto a major road. Neighbours have also complained about noise from ordering speakers late at night.

Restaurant owners argue that the rules ignore the needs of some customers. Parents with young children in car seats, people with disabilities and seniors with limited mobility often rely on drive-throughs. Some owners also note that drive-through sales can make up more than half of a fast-food restaurant’s revenue, so a ban can make a new location unprofitable. They also point out that drive-through customers are often in a hurry and would simply go elsewhere rather than park and walk in. A few owners have even offered to pay for traffic studies themselves if it means their projects can go ahead.

Planners are experimenting with compromises. Some new restaurants use pickup windows for orders placed in advance through an app, which shortens lines and reduces idling. Others are designed so that cars wait in a lane on the restaurant’s own property, well away from the street. Several cities now allow existing drive-throughs to continue but require any new ones to include space for at least twelve cars. Some planners argue that, in the long run, better transit and walkable neighbourhoods will reduce demand for drive-throughs on their own. Others doubt this will happen quickly.

p4.title: Let Them Walk
p4.byline: Opinion | by Carmen Ruiz, parent and journalist
p4.text:
When I was nine, I walked one kilometre to school every day with my younger brother. Nobody thought anything of it. Today, in my neighbourhood, I almost never see children walking alone. Every morning, the street outside our elementary school is jammed with cars, idling and double-parked, as parents drop off children who live, in many cases, a few blocks away.

I understand the instinct. We have all heard frightening stories, and no parent wants to take a risk with their child’s safety. But the data tells a different story from the one we imagine. Crimes against children by strangers are extremely rare, and have not increased over the past several decades. The greatest danger to children walking to school is traffic, and the heaviest traffic around schools is, ironically, created by parents driving their children. In one survey, most parents said they would let their children walk if other children on the street did too, which suggests the problem is partly one of habit.

Meanwhile, the costs of driving everywhere are real. Children who walk or bike to school are more physically active, and studies suggest they arrive more alert and ready to learn. Fewer cars at the school gate also means cleaner air for the children who are already walking. Walking alone also builds independence and judgment, skills that cannot be learned from the back seat of a car. A child who has navigated their own route, crossed streets carefully and dealt with small problems arrives at adolescence far better prepared than one who has never been unsupervised.

This is not to say that every child should be sent out the door on their own. Age, maturity, distance and the safety of the route all matter. A seven-year-old crossing a four-lane road is not the same as a ten-year-old walking three quiet blocks. Parents can start gradually: walk together for a few weeks, then let the child walk the last block alone, and expand from there. Walking with a friend or a group of neighbourhood children adds both safety and fun.

Schools and cities have a role too. Crossing guards, lower speed limits near schools and “school streets,” where cars are banned at drop-off and pick-up times, make walking safer for everyone. Some schools organize “walking school buses,” in which a parent volunteer walks a set route and children join along the way. In a few communities, shops along popular routes have even put stickers in their windows to show children they can stop in if they need help.

Our children are more capable than we often give them credit for. Let’s give them back the walk to school.

qs.x: Carmen argues children should be given back the walk to school, starting gradually and considering age and route. She does not want every child sent out alone or parents to stop driving entirely.

t2.intro: Your city is planning its Canada Day celebration and can afford only one evening event.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: A traditional fireworks display over the river.
t2.b: A drone light show, in which hundreds of lit drones create moving pictures in the sky.
t2.model:
I would choose Option B, the drone light show, because I believe it would be safer, kinder to the environment and more memorable for our community.

First of all, fireworks create a lot of noise and smoke. Many residents, including veterans, young children and people with sensory sensitivities, find the loud explosions distressing, and pet owners know how terrified dogs become. A drone show is almost silent, so everyone could enjoy the evening.

Second, fireworks leave debris in the river and release chemicals into the air, and in dry summers they can even cause fires. Drones can be reused year after year, and they create no smoke or litter.

Most importantly, a drone show can tell a story. Instead of random explosions of colour, drones could form a maple leaf, a canoe or the outline of our city’s historic bridge, and they could even honour local volunteers or Indigenous history. That would make the celebration feel truly connected to our community.

I understand that fireworks are a tradition, and some people may be disappointed. However, I think most residents would quickly come to appreciate a show that is quieter, cleaner and more creative.

t1.prompt: Your friend is forty years old and is thinking about going back to school full-time to study nursing. She has a stable office job and two teenage children. Give her advice.
t1.model: I think that’s a really brave and exciting idea, and honestly, forty is a great age to make a change – you could still have a twenty-five-year nursing career ahead of you. But I’d think about a few things first. The biggest one is money. A nursing program is usually two to four years, and if you study full-time, you’ll lose your salary. Sit down with your partner and work out exactly how long your savings would last. Look into student loans and grants too, because mature students are often eligible for more than they expect. Second, check whether you could study part-time or online at first, at least for the prerequisite courses like biology and chemistry. That way you could keep working for the first year and make sure you really enjoy it. Third, talk to your kids. As teenagers, they can help more at home, and they might actually be proud of you. Finally, I’d try to volunteer at a hospital or shadow a nurse for a day, just to see the reality of the job, including the night shifts. If you still love it after that, I say go for it!

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you were really surprised. What happened, and how did you react?
t2.model: One of the biggest surprises of my life happened on my thirtieth birthday. I had just moved to Halifax for work, and I didn’t know many people yet, so I was expecting a quiet evening. My new colleague, Sam, invited me for dinner at a small restaurant near the waterfront, which I thought was really nice of her. When we walked in, the room suddenly went dark, then the lights came on, and there were about fifteen people shouting “Surprise!” At first, I didn’t even understand what was happening. Then I saw my older brother, who lives in Toronto, and my best friend from university, who had flown in from Calgary. Sam had contacted them through social media without me knowing and organized everything. I was so shocked that I just stood there with my mouth open, and then I started crying, which everyone found very funny. It meant so much to me, because I had been feeling quite lonely in a new city. That night, I realized I was already starting to build a real community here, and Sam is still one of my closest friends.

On the left-hand side, there’s an orange tent set up near a pine tree, and right next to it there’s a small campfire. A man in a grey T-shirt is sitting beside the fire, relaxing – maybe he’s waiting to cook dinner. In the middle of the picture, there’s a wooden picnic table with a blue cooler on it, and a woman with long hair and a red top is standing next to it, looking at a map, so she’s probably planning tomorrow’s hike. Out on the lake, two people are paddling an orange canoe – one is wearing green and the other blue. On the right-hand side, near the shore, a child in a yellow shirt is holding what looks like a fishing rod, and a brown dog is lying next to him. There are also two ducks swimming near the shore. It looks like a really peaceful, relaxing family camping trip.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think a few things will happen soon. First, since the sun seems to be going down and the man is already sitting by the fire, they’ll probably start cooking dinner soon – maybe hot dogs or burgers – and then roast marshmallows for dessert. The woman with the map will most likely put it away and help get the food out of the cooler. Second, the people in the canoe will probably paddle back to shore before it gets dark, because it’s not safe to be on the water at night. Third, the child who is fishing might actually catch a small fish. If he does, he’ll be really excited, and the dog will probably jump up and start barking, which might scare the ducks away. I’d guess the parents will tell him to let the fish go. Finally, later in the evening, they’ll probably all sit around the campfire together, telling stories, before going to sleep in the tent.

t5.persuade: Your partner prefers buying a second car. Persuade your partner that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know a second car would be more comfortable, especially in the winter, but I really think the transit pass is the smarter choice for us. Let’s start with the money. The car is eighteen thousand dollars, and then there’s three hundred and thirty a month just for parking and insurance, before gas and repairs. The transit pass is a hundred and twenty-eight a month, and that’s it. Over a year, we’d save at least three thousand dollars on monthly costs alone – that’s a great family vacation. Second, the time difference is really small. The car is twenty minutes in normal traffic, but downtown at rush hour, it’s rarely normal. The bus and train take thirty-five minutes, but that’s time I can use to read, answer emails or just relax instead of sitting in traffic stressed out. And the service runs every ten minutes, so I don’t have to plan my whole day around a schedule. Finally, if we have one car instead of two, we use it for weekends and family trips, and we’re doing something good for the environment too. Can we try the pass for three months and see how it goes?

t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hey Ethan, can we talk for a few minutes? I want to talk about last night. You came home at one in the morning, two hours after the time we agreed on, and you didn’t call or answer my texts. I’m not trying to be dramatic, but I was really worried. I didn’t know where you were, I couldn’t reach you, and I was about to call your friends’ parents. Your mom and dad trusted me to look after you this summer, and if anything had happened, I would never forgive myself. I also want to hear your side, though. Did something happen? Did your phone die, or did you lose track of time? I understand that you’re sixteen and you want more freedom, and I’m not trying to treat you like a little kid. So here’s what I suggest. The curfew stays at eleven, but if you’re ever going to be late, you call me before eleven – no excuses – and we can talk about it. If you do that, I don’t need to tell your parents about last night. But if it happens again without a call, I’ll have to. Does that sound fair?

t7.prompt: Answer the following question: Should all single-use plastic bags be banned in stores? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: In my opinion, yes, single-use plastic bags should be banned in stores, as long as affordable alternatives are available. My main reason is the environment. Plastic bags are used for maybe twenty minutes, but they can take hundreds of years to break down. They end up in rivers, lakes and oceans, where animals mistake them for food. Even in Canada, where we have recycling programs, most plastic bags are never actually recycled because they jam the sorting machines. Secondly, people adapt very quickly. When my city started charging for bags a few years ago, everyone complained for a month, and now almost everyone brings reusable bags without thinking about it. A ban would simply finish that process. Of course, some people argue that paper bags and heavy reusable bags have their own environmental costs, and that’s true if they’re only used once or twice. That’s why the key is to encourage people to reuse bags many times. Stores could also offer cheap or free reusable bags to low-income customers. Overall, I believe a ban is a simple, practical step that would reduce a very visible kind of pollution.

scene.alt: A blue city bus labelled "ROUTE 12" with a vegetable garden growing on its roof. There is a long wooden planter box along the whole roof, with green plants, red tomatoes and yellow flowers, and a small clear greenhouse-like shelter at the centre. The bus is stopped at a bus stop, and passengers are getting on. A man on the sidewalk is pointing up at the roof garden.

t8.prompt: You see this unusual bus in your city. Call a friend who lives in another city and describe the bus. Explain whether you think it is a good idea. Your friend cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hey Sara! You have to hear about this. I’m standing at a bus stop downtown, and a city bus just pulled up with a vegetable garden on its roof. I’m not joking. It’s a normal blue bus – Route 12 – but along the entire roof, there’s a long wooden planter box, and it’s full of green plants. I can see red tomatoes, some yellow flowers and what look like herbs or lettuce. In the middle of the roof, there’s a small clear shelter, a bit like a mini greenhouse. People are getting on as usual, and a man next to me is pointing up at it and laughing. I asked the driver, and he said it’s a city pilot project. The plants help keep the bus cooler in summer, so they use less air conditioning, and the vegetables are donated to a food bank. Honestly, I think it’s a brilliant idea. It makes people smile, it’s good for the environment, and it gets people talking about green spaces. My only question is how they water it, and what happens in winter. Maybe they take the plants off? Anyway, I think your city should try it too!
